extracted.intended_audience: political leaders, constitutional framers, and educated public (late-18th-century American context)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and institutional requirements for drafting and evaluating republican constitutions (especially American state/national constitutions) as argued by John Adams; covers separation of powers, representation, local institutions, militia, and education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers (executive from legislative and judicial)
rubrics_metrics.description: A total separation of the executive from the legislative power, and of the judicial from both; a balance in the legislature by three independent, equal branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly emphasized as a foundational structural requirement: 'a total Reparation of the executive from the legiflative power, and of the judicial from both' and 'three independent, equal branches.' Presented as necessary to prevent corruption of the legislature and preserve people's rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong executive required
rubrics_metrics.description: The people's rights and liberties, and the democratical mixture in a constitution, can never be preserved without a strong executive; or, in other words, without separating the executive power from the legislative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues against simple or weak executives: a strong, separate executive is necessary to prevent the corruption and decay of liberties even in democratically-mixed constitutions. The executive must be independent of the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance in the legislature by three branches
rubrics_metrics.description: A balance in the legislature, by three independent, equal branches (implying an upper chamber, a popular chamber, and a separate executive/judicial arrangement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as one of the core innovations for free government and as protection against factional swings and the instabilities seen in ancient republics; likened to musical harmony when arranged skillfully, and to terrible discord when confused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal representation rule (numbers, property, or both)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equal representation, of which numbers, or property, or both would be the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The end in forming a representative assembly is to capture 'the sense of the people' — proportions of electors and members are 'an affair of calculation.' The choice between numbers, property, or a mix should be selected to faithfully portrait the public voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of office / frequency of elections
rubrics_metrics.description: The duration must not be so long that the deputy would have time to forget the opinions of his constituents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elections should be frequent enough to prevent representatives from becoming disconnected or corrupted by influence; duration is a design parameter to ensure accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preventing corruption in elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Corruption in elections is the great enemy of freedom. Among provisions to prevent it: more frequent elections, a more general privilege of voting, dividing the districts, diminishing the distance of travel, and confining the choice to residents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives concrete anti-corruption measures: reduce travel burdens, localize districts, expand franchise, increase election frequency. Emphasizes practical administrative choices (districting, travel distance) as means to reduce bribery and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate upper chamber (senate) to moderate elite influence
rubrics_metrics.description: The rich, the well-born, and the able acquire an influence among the people that will soon be too much for simple honesty in a house of representatives; they must therefore be separated from the mass, and placed by themselves in a senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the senate as a place to absorb elite ambition safely and to make it the object of ambition; the senate takes much of elite influence out of direct popular assemblies, acting as a check while preserving incentives for public service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentrating executive power in assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: If the executive power, or any considerable part of it, is left in the hands either of an aristocratical or a democratical assembly, it will corrupt the legislature as necessarily as rust corrupts iron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that placing executive functions within legislatures—whether aristocratic or democratic—inevitably leads to corruption of the legislative body and destruction of public liberty; institution design must keep executive functions distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local towns/districts as foundational political units
rubrics_metrics.description: Towns or districts are corporations invested with powers and privileges (repair roads, maintain poor, elect officers, instruct their representatives), and are where popular sentiments are first formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that local corporate town government habituates citizens to deliberate public affairs, forming public opinion and grounding representation; district boundaries and local corporate rights are therefore central design choices for a stable republic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious societies (churches) as popular institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Churches are religious societies comprising the people; ministers are chosen by the people of their parish and have little formal authority, being dependent on the parish for position and reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents churches as civic institutions that promote virtue and liberty: clergy live among parishioners, exercise charity, and are socially accountable; this popular character of churches supports civil liberty rather than clerical domination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public education requirement (town schools)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are schools in every town: each town consisting in sixty families is obliged under penalty to maintain constantly a school and a master who teaches reading, writing, arithmetic, & the principles of Latin & Greek.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education is treated as a legal obligation placed on towns to ensure broad literacy and to prepare youth for colleges and public office; schools are a deliberate institutional foundation for republican competency and leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia organization and citizen readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The militia comprises all the people: every male between 16 and 60 is enrolled in a company and regiment, obliged to keep a musket, powder, shot, cartridge-box, & haversack; companies must assemble at set times for inspection and manoeuvres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Militia law binds citizenry to common defense and fosters military habit and courage among the populace. It is presented both as practical defense policy and as a civic virtue supporting republican independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances to prevent factional violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Without three orders and an effectual balance between them in every American constitution, it must be destined to frequent unavoidable revolutions; checks and balances prevent the factions and massacres seen in Greek history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses historical examples (Greece) to argue that institutional balance (multiple orders/branches) prevents cycles of faction, revenge, and civil slaughter; design should intentionally create equilibrium among interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional apportionment as a calculable design parameter
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportions of electors and members is an affair of calculation; numbers, or property, or both, would be the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames representation as an engineering problem: apportionment must be calculated with attention to local conditions and objectives (e.g., fidelity to public voice), rather than left to vague principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy grounded in reason and common religion, not divine right
rubrics_metrics.description: These governments were contrived merely by the use of reason and the senses... it will be for ever acknowledged that these governments were contrived merely by the use of reason and the senses... authority in magistrates and obedience of citizens can be grounded on reason, morality, and the Christian religion, without the monkery of priests, or the knavery of politicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects claims that laws must be presented as divinely revealed; legitimacy should be constructed on rational and moral grounds. Constitutional design should aim for transparency and rational foundations rather than mystical assertions of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of a democratical branch is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no free government without a democratical branch in the constitution; democratical mixtures in government are essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insists that at least one branch must be democratically based to ensure popular voice; but this democratic element must be balanced by other institutions (senate, executive) to prevent tyranny of faction and corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive secrecy and dispatch attainable in free government
rubrics_metrics.description: Secrecy, where the executive is entire in one hand, is as easily and surely preserved in a free government as in a simple monarchy; and as to dispatch, English history furnishes many examples of efficient action under free institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responds to objections that republican systems cannot preserve secrecy or act decisively: properly designed republican institutions can achieve necessary executive confidentiality and timeliness of action.
